ASTRA — Chemical Transformation: Controlling Multi-Reactant Chemistry

Research continuation · 24 October 2026

1. New direction: Controlling reaction order instead of merely reaction rate

I am moving the active investigation away from Fe(OEP). Its established SH2S_H2SH​2 chemistry, fragment/site-memory distinction, storage-capacity limit, optical interference and regeneration requirements remain useful prior work. However, another refinement of organoiron survival would not presently establish a new manufacturing operation.

The new research question is:

Can a catalyst selectively accumulate and combine several reactive intermediates, even when their arrivals are too sparse or mismatched for conventional simultaneous chemistry?

A consequential application is manufacturing urea from CO₂ and nitrate-containing waste streams.

Urea requires one carbon atom and two nitrogen atoms. Ordinary electrochemical nitrate reduction strongly competes with ammonia formation, while successful urea formation requires the nitrogen and carbon intermediates to encounter one another in the correct chemical states.

Why this is a serious scientific opening

Two important primary studies published in 2026 establish complementary chemical mechanisms:

Mo–Mn diatomic catalyst — Science Advances, May 2026

Researchers identified a pathway involving two adsorbed nitric oxide intermediates forming an N–N-containing species, followed by CO insertion. They reported 93.3% nitrogen selectivity toward urea, 48.1% Faradaic efficiency and 35.16 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ urea production. The N–N-mediated pathway is their finding, not my invention.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

Ag/CdO catalyst — Nature Communications, January 2026

Researchers reported early coupling of carbon- and nitrogen-containing intermediates, including a proposed *CONO₂ state. Their optimized two-electrode system reached 59.1% Faradaic efficiency at approximately 60 mA/cm², and remained operational for 1,000 hours, although urea production declined to approximately 75% of its initial rate.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

These are already substantial experimental achievements. The question is not whether urea electrosynthesis is possible. It is whether a more general mechanism can control when an intermediate commits to a multi-atom product rather than escaping into a competing reaction.

Both studies predominantly investigate relatively concentrated nitrate electrolytes. The Mo–Mn article specifies 50 mM in one experimental description and 100 mM in its general electrochemical methods, an inconsistency that should be resolved before quantitative reproduction. The Ag/CdO two-electrode study used 50 mM nitrate and 1 M KOH. Neither establishes equivalent selectivity at 1 mM nitrate.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
+1

That low-concentration regime is the first target, not because it guarantees a commercial opportunity, but because it exposes a fundamental problem in reaction kinetics.

A. Every urea molecule requires two nitrate-derived nitrogen atoms

The overall acidic half-reaction is

Consequently, even a perfect catalyst cannot manufacture urea faster than half the incoming molar nitrate flux.

The reported 60 mA/cm², 59.1%-FE experiment corresponds to approximately 82.7 µmol cm⁻² h⁻¹ of urea. This is comparable to the illustrative 50 mM diffusion ceiling, but that agreement does not establish the actual experimental mass-transfer limitation.

At 1 mM, sustaining the same nitrate consumption flux through a simple diffusion layer would require an effective diffusion distance of approximately 2.18 µm, instead of 100 µm.

Thus a highly selective catalyst cannot eliminate the need for adequate transport, electrode area, flow-through access or concentration management.

For a 16-electron product formed at full-cell voltage VVV and Faradaic efficiency fff,

Using the reported operating values of 1.6 V and 59.1% Faradaic efficiency yields approximately

19.3 kWh/kg of urea.\boxed{19.3\ \mathrm{kWh/kg\ of\ urea}}.19.3 kWh/kg of urea​.

This is the electrical input associated with the reported operating point, not a measured total life-cycle energy figure. It excludes nitrate production, CO₂ supply, pumping, separation, electrolyte management and capital costs.

Any genuinely consequential architecture must ultimately improve useful output per unit of matter, charge and energy, not just a spectroscopic selectivity metric.

These constraints make the central opportunity more precise: improve chemical selectivity at low intermediate flux without disguising reactant concentration, residence time or applied power as free resources.

3. First foundational result: Why ordinary cooperative binding eventually fails at low concentration

The Mo–Mn study suggests a mechanism based on two nearby NO-derived intermediates. The important quantity is therefore not simply average NO coverage. It is the probability that the correct pair of sites is simultaneously occupied.

For a coupled reaction requiring both intermediates, the elementary reaction rate is proportional to P11P_{11}P11​, not merely xxx.

This creates a dilute-feed problem: halving a small coverage reduces independently paired occupancy by a factor of four.

The deeper result appears in the dilute limit:

Finite, fixed adsorption cooperativity cannot eliminate the quadratic dependence of equilibrium pair formation on sufficiently dilute reactant activity.

It can shift the useful operating concentration substantially, but it does not change the asymptotic reaction order.

This is the first failed mechanism in the new investigation: simply making two neighbouring adsorption sites more cooperative is not a concentration-independent solution.

To change the low-concentration scaling, a system needs a different physical operation. One possibility is retaining the first captured intermediate long enough for the second arrival, instead of requiring two intermediates to coexist through ordinary adsorption equilibrium.

I am proposing a kinetic rather than purely equilibrium architecture.

The reaction ensemble has three principal states:

A minimal kinetic state machine. State 2 also has a competing waste-product exit; these are proposed effective states, not an experimentally resolved catalyst sequence.

The first nitrogen-derived intermediate arrives at rate λ1\lambda_1λ1​ per empty gate. It remains available until a second intermediate arrives at rate λ2\lambda_2λ2​, or is lost irreversibly at rate μ\muμ.

Once two nitrogen fragments are committed to a paired state, productive CO insertion and release occurs with rate kpk_pkp​, while an unwanted two-nitrogen pathway occurs with rate kwk_wkw​.

The proposed physical implementation would start with the already demonstrated Mo–Mn nitrogen-pair chemistry. The required advance is an independently stabilized one-N state that suppresses further reduction to ammonia without preventing the next N capture, followed by rapid CO insertion and site regeneration.

The Mo–Mn paper provides suggestive evidence: stronger NO adsorption than its Cu–Mn comparator, spectroscopic NO–NO and N–N-related intermediates, and CO-related reaction intermediates. But its temperature-programmed desorption data and DFT energies do not determine the relevant first-N survival rate or the coupled kinetic constants.

Physical scope

The optimal-density law is exact for the specified Markov model, not a universal law of heterogeneous catalysis. In particular, the assumed fixed flux 
𝐽
J may change when active-site density changes. Reactants can also migrate between sites, become trapped in other surface states or be redirected toward vacant sites.

An equally capable reactor using adaptive transport may outperform this restricted model.

Nevertheless, the derived law gives a genuinely testable scientific proposition:

For reactions with persistent intermediate capture and finite-state occupancy, deliberately reducing the number of active reaction ensembles can improve product formation at fixed reactant delivery, until capacity saturation reverses the advantage.

A catalyst need not have the largest number of sites to make the most useful product.

This suggests a physical design direction: concentrate activated reactant arrival onto a controlled population of productive pairing sites, rather than distributing it indiscriminately across the largest possible catalytic surface.

6. Connecting the theory to physical chemistry

The strongest experimentally grounded starting point remains the Mo–Mn diatomic structure, rather than an invented molecular host.

The physical requirements are now more precise.

First-N state: chemically protected, not permanently poisoned

Adsorbed NO must survive further reduction, desorption and parasitic hydrogenation over the interval between reactant arrivals. Reversible excursions that preserve usable nitrogen inventory must be distinguished from irreversible nitrogen loss.

Second-N capture: state-dependent access

A singly occupied ensemble must remain accessible to the next nitrogen intermediate. Favorable first-N adsorption is insufficient if it blocks the geometric or electronic pathway for second-N capture.

Paired-state readout: CO insertion before nitrogen loss

A delayed cross-label response could indicate retained reactive nitrogen, but it would not alone prove N–N dimerization. Sequential C–N chemistry could also incorporate nitrogen atoms arriving at different times. Discriminating the mechanisms would additionally require intermediate-specific spectroscopy, calibrated electrolyte exchange times and isotope neutrality controls.

The decisive physical quantities are the lifetime of the first nitrogen state, the flux of successful second captures, the productive probability of the paired state, and the recovery of active catalyst after product release.

The model makes a further discriminating prediction: if incident activated-nitrogen flux stays fixed while the number of accessible pairing sites changes, product flux can exhibit an interior maximum rather than increasing monotonically with site density.

Failure of this prediction under conditions satisfying the delivery assumptions would challenge the proposed kinetic model. Strong flux redistribution or changes in catalytic-site identity would instead invalidate the simplifying assumptions, not necessarily the underlying idea of sequential capture.

10. Research checkpoint

The new investigation has produced three connected findings.

A finite-equilibrium-cooperativity limit: Stronger neighbouring-site binding alone cannot remove the asymptotically quadratic dilute-concentration dependence of equilibrium pair occupancy.

A sequential-capture principle: A sufficiently persistent first intermediate can convert a two-arrival reaction from quadratic dilute-feed behaviour into first-order, supply-limited behaviour, without violating material conservation.

An optimal active-site-density law: Under a specified finite-state capture model, the optimal pairing-site density is

It exposes a physical tradeoff between crowding, reactive-state survival and readout rate, rather than treating maximal catalyst loading as automatically favourable.

These derivations are analytically established within their stated models and were checked by numerical stationary-state calculations. Their historical novelty, and applicability to the real electrochemical interface, remain unresolved.

The central chemical hypothesis is that productive manufacture of multi-reactant molecules can be controlled by engineering the correlation and persistence of partially assembled states—not solely their mean coverage, binding strength or instantaneous reaction rate.

The strongest next research problem is now well defined: determine whether the experimentally supported N–N-first or C–N-first urea pathway possesses a long-lived, chemically accessible intermediate that can make use of this kinetic principle under a single operating regime.

If neither pathway supports that state, the correct conclusion is not to add an arbitrary molecular host. It is to retain the reaction-order and site-density theory, reject that particular physical implementation, and search for a transformation where a persistent partial product is more strongly warranted.

That would preserve a potentially general chemical-control framework while keeping its distinction from an acquired manufacturing technology explicit.
